tagline: Switchbacks climb from desert plants to forests of pine, spruce and fir
intro: Swift Trail climbs from cactus, yucca and mesquite into the high forests of the Pinaleño Mountains. The winding road rises from 2,900 feet in the Gila Valley to ridges at 9,000 feet. Part of SR 366 is designated Swift Trail Parkway under Arizona’s Parkways, Historic and Scenic Roads program. The Forest Service compares its changing life zones to a drive from Mexico to Canada and suggests around five hours for the round trip, plus side trips. These mountains are called Sky Islands because desert separates their high forests from neighboring ranges. The Pinaleños are the highest of southeastern Arizona’s Sky Islands.

Named for T. T. Swift, the Coronado National Forest’s first supervisor, the route was constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps during the Great Depression. Workers based at Columbine extended it to Riggs Flat Lake while developing mountain campgrounds and trails. SR 366 followed in 1960, initially as a gravel highway; its lower portion was later paved.

From US 191 south of Safford, the climb leads through oak grasslands and pinyon-juniper woodland into pine, spruce and fir. Five hairpins mark Turkey Flat. Beyond Columbine Visitor Center, forest roads continue to Riggs Flat Lake, set among alpine forest and meadow.

moments.title: Turkey Flat
moments.text: Five hairpin turns carry SR 366 through Turkey Flat as the highway follows the mountain terrain. The nearby dispersed camping area sits in open ponderosa pine forest at 7,400 feet. A 0.3-mile trail connects that campground with Ladybug Trail.

moments.title: Columbine
moments.text: Columbine Visitor Center began as a ranger station residence, built around 1935 by the Civilian Conservation Corps. The residence was part of a larger work station whose other buildings were also constructed by CCC crews. The Columbine camp operated in summer, and its workers extended Swift Trail to Riggs Flat Lake and developed campgrounds and trails. The residence now houses exhibits on the area’s natural and cultural history. Its gabled roof, multipaned windows and lapped siding reflect the Forest Service’s Depression-era architecture. Beside the building, a paved interpretive path follows the edge of an alpine meadow.
moments.notice: Look for the gabled roof, multipaned windows and lapped siding of the former ranger residence.

moments.title: Riggs Flat Lake
moments.text: Swift Trail ends at Riggs Flat Lake, an 11-acre lake set in alpine forest and meadow high in the Pinaleños. Workers from the Columbine CCC camp extended the road here. The approach beyond Columbine Visitor Center follows Forest Roads 803 and 287. Brown and rainbow trout are stocked in the cold water during summer. West Peak is visible from the lake’s vicinity, while a short hike to an overlook gives views west to Aravaipa Valley and the Galiuro Mountains. Winter closes the vehicle approach, and early or late snow can lengthen the season when the lake is inaccessible by road.

practical: Riggs Flat Lake: Vehicle access closes November 15 to April 15; early or late snow may extend the closure. Vehicles including trailers longer than 22 feet are not recommended on the switchbacks. (checked 2026-10-11)
